arpc.title: Average revenue per customer (ARPC)
arpc.content:
ARPC is TradeWindow's own disclosed monthly revenue per active customer, reported separately for its two segments: shippers (exporters/importers) and freight forwarders/customs brokers. It is not derived from Revenue/ActiveCustomers in this CSV -- the company publishes the segment split directly.

For TradeWindow: both segments have been compounding at roughly 20% per period (shippers $1,944 to $2,484/mo, freight forwarders $824 to $1,097/mo between H1 FY25 and H1 FY26) even as the total customer count has been flat to declining. This is the crux of the bull/bear split: growth is coming from existing customers adopting more modules and re-pricing, not from net new logos -- durable if it reflects genuine cross-sell, fragile if it is concentration into fewer, larger accounts.

What to watch:

  • ARPC growth continuing to outpace (or merely offset) any decline in Active Customers
  • Whether freight-forwarder ARPC, the newer and smaller segment, keeps closing the gap on shippers
  • Re-pricing versus genuine module cross-sell as the driver

retention.title: Customer retention and active customers
retention.content:
Customer Retention Rate is the company's own disclosed metric for the share of customers retained period-on-period. Plotted alongside Active Customers, the total customer count at period end.

For TradeWindow: retention swung from 97% (H1 FY25) to 87% (FY25) to 92% (H1 FY26) -- management says the FY25 drop was a deliberate pruning of low-value accounts, but the qualitative risk write-up flags this volatility as a named risk, and the total customer base has been flat-to-declining (554 → 534) even as retention recovered. Read this chart together with the ARPC chart: rising ARPC with a shrinking or flat customer base means growth is now concentrated in fewer, larger accounts.

What to watch:

  • Retention stabilising above 90% rather than oscillating
  • Active Customers returning to growth, not just ARPC
  • Any disclosed reason for a retention move (pricing action versus involuntary churn)

shareIssuance.title: Share issuance proceeds
shareIssuance.content:
Share issuance proceeds is cash raised from issuing new shares in the period (placements, SPPs, option exercises) -- a financing inflow, not an operating result.

For TradeWindow: this is the funding side of the dilution risk called out in both the qualitative analysis and the DCF: the FY2023 raise (NZ$14.7m, itself only 27% of a NZ$20m target) is the largest bar shown, but the company has also raised since every FY-end in this chart's window -- an ~NZ$5.8m placement settled 15-Dec-2025 and an ~NZ$5.9m SPP that closed 13-Feb-2026, both after FY2025 and not yet reflected here. The DCF's base case implies at least one further raise is needed before the business is self-funding.

What to watch:

  • Raises sized relative to the existing share count (dilution rate), not just the dollar amount
  • Whether future raises are needed to fund FreightAI or simply to survive
  • Proceeds achieved versus the target size of the raise (2023's shortfall is the cautionary precedent)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For TradeWindow Holdings Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
